territorial_scope.description: Applies to food producers and coordinators acting in or affecting United States commerce, enforced by federal and state officials.

evidence.quote: It is unlawful for a food producer, in or affecting commerce, or any agent or subcontractor thereof

summary.short: Prohibits food producers from exchanging value for the services of a 'coordinator' that runs algorithmic price or supply coordination, and bars coordinators from facilitating non-competition agreements among food producers. Enforced by the FTC, the Attorney General and state attorneys general, with treble-damages private suits. No effective date is stated.
summary.long: The bill defines 'coordinating function' as collecting price or supply data from two or more food producers, analysing it with software or algorithms (including to train an algorithm), and recommending food prices, supply, output or other commercial terms to a food producer. Sec. 3(a)(1) makes it unlawful for a food producer, in or affecting commerce, to subscribe to, contract with, or otherwise exchange value for a coordinator's services, and deems this a per se violation of the Sherman Act. Sec. 3(a)(2) makes it unlawful for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among food producers not to compete on prices, supply, output or other commercial terms. Sec. 4(a) assigns enforcement to the FTC (including civil penalties in its own name), the Attorney General and state attorneys general, and treats a violation as an unfair method of competition. Sec. 4(a)(4) lets a complaint plausibly plead a violation by alleging consciously parallel pricing coordination. Sec. 4(b) allows any aggrieved person to sue for threefold damages and litigation costs, and lets the plaintiff void pre-dispute arbitration agreements and joint action waivers. Sec. 5 preserves the antitrust laws, Sec. 6 does not preempt state laws that supplement the Act, and Sec. 7 is a severability clause. The text states no effective date.},

relations.note: Sec. 3(a)(1) deems a violation of the contract-or-conspiracy prohibition a per se violation of the Sherman Act. Sec. 4(a)(4)(A) also pleads a violation of section 1 or 3(a) of the Sherman Act. Sec. 4(a)(1)(B) and (C) incorporate its terms for enforcement.

evidence.quote: and such action shall be deemed to be a per se violation of the Sherman Act (15 U.S.C. 1 et seq.)

relations.target_text: Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.)
relations.note: Sec. 4(a)(1)(A) gives the FTC enforcement powers as though the FTC Act's applicable terms were incorporated into this Act. Sec. 4(a)(2) also treats a violation as an unfair method of competition under section 5 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 45).

evidence.quote: as though all applicable terms of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.) were incorporated into and made a part of this Act

relations.note: Sec. 4(a)(1)(B) and (C) incorporate its applicable terms for enforcement by the Attorney General and State attorneys general. Sec. 2(8) also takes the definition of 'person' from section 1 of the Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. 12).

notes: Standalone bill. No provision amends, repeals, implements or transposes an existing statute, and no enabling act is cited, so no legal_basis, amends or repeal relations are recorded. All relations are references to external US statutes, applied by incorporation (Sec. 4(a)(1)) or by definition (Sec. 2(6)). Sec. 5 refers to 'any amendment made by this Act', but the bill contains no amendments. Target instrument IDs are empty because the annotator did not have registry IDs for these statutes.

events.note: The bill text contains no dates, no entry-into-force or effective-date provision, no application, deadline, sunset or repeal provisions, and no legislative history. The registry lists legislative_stage as introduced, but no introduction date appears in the fetched text and no official legislature URL was supplied, so no external event was recorded.

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff changing legal treatment was found. The text defines conduct by a plurality ('2 or more food producers' in Sec. 2(3) and 2(4)(A)), which is part of a definition rather than a size, value or scope cutoff, so it is not coded. Treble damages in Sec. 4(b)(2)(A) are a remedy, and no dollar, size or volume tests appear.
